# PDE theory: why the architecture looks the way it does {#sec-pde-theory}

Every structural choice in this program — global attention, quadrature
weighting, drive linearity, the density-solve factorization, even the sign of
a relaxation parameter — is forced by classical potential theory. This
chapter collects that theory in one place, developed for Laplace where
everything is explicit. Because the product scope (see the problem statement
in the front matter) does not supply the governing equations, the closing
section separates which parts of this story are PDE-agnostic — and may
therefore be assumed in deployment — from which are properties of the known
fundamental solution.

## The solution operator

Consider the interior Dirichlet problem on a bounded domain
$\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^D$ with smooth boundary $\Gamma = \partial\Omega$:

$$
\Delta u = 0 \ \text{ in } \Omega,
\qquad u = g \ \text{ on } \Gamma.
$$

At fixed geometry the solution map $g \mapsto u$ is **linear**: for any
$\alpha, \beta$,

$$
\mathcal N_\Gamma(\alpha g_1 + \beta g_2)
= \alpha\,\mathcal N_\Gamma(g_1) + \beta\,\mathcal N_\Gamma(g_2),
\qquad \mathcal N_\Gamma(0) = 0.
$$

A surrogate that violates this (through softmax normalization, biases in the
field path, or amplitude-dependent activations) is wrong before it sees any
data. The `linear` field mode of @sec-mesh-attention and every
boundary-integral model of @sec-learned-bie preserve it exactly.

## Green representation and its two readings

For $u$ harmonic in $\Omega$ and $G$ the free-space fundamental solution
($G = -\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\log|x-y|$ in 2D, $G = \tfrac{1}{4\pi|x-y|}$ in 3D),
Green's third identity gives, for $x \in \Omega$,

$$
u(x)=\int_{\Gamma}
\Bigl[G(x,y)\,\partial_{n_y}u(y)
-u(y)\,\partial_{n_y}G(x,y)\Bigr]\,dS_y.
$$ {#eq-green}

Two consequences drive the architecture.

### Reading 1: harmonic measure and global information flow {#sec-global-flow}

For the Dirichlet problem,

$$
u(x) = \int_\Gamma g(y)\, d\omega_x(y),
$$

where $\omega_x$ is harmonic measure. On a regular domain it has a
Poisson-kernel density with respect to $dS$, and — critically — that density
depends on the *whole domain*, not on $x - y$ and $n_y$ alone. Every boundary
patch influences every interior point, with no cutoff radius that remains
valid after a change of geometry. This is why the program excludes graph neighborhoods,
distance envelopes, and near/far truncations: for connected elliptic problems
the correct inductive bias is **all-to-all**, and locality is a numerical
acceleration concern (FMM, $\mathcal H$-matrices), never a modeling
assumption.

### Reading 2: quadrature against boundary measure

Both terms in @eq-green are integrals against $dS_y$. A discrete surrogate must therefore
weight source contributions by cell measure — replacing one panel by two
half-panels must leave the operator unchanged. Every source contraction in
the stack carries `cell_areas`; unit weights are never substituted.

## Layer potentials and the second-kind structure

The representation @eq-green suggests an ansatz. Writing the double-layer
potential with density $\mu$,

$$
(\mathcal D\mu)(x) = \int_\Gamma \partial_{n_y}G(x,y)\,\mu(y)\,dS_y,
$$

the **jump relations** state that as $x \to x_0 \in \Gamma$ from inside,

$$
(\mathcal D\mu)(x) \;\longrightarrow\; \pm\tfrac12\,\mu(x_0) + (K\mu)(x_0),
$$

where $K$ is the boundary restriction of $\mathcal D$ (a principal value) and
the sign is a convention/orientation choice. Imposing the boundary condition
turns the PDE into a **boundary integral equation (BIE)**:

$$
\bigl(\tfrac12 I + K\bigr)\,\mu = g .
$$ {#eq-bie}

On a smooth boundary $K$ is compact, so @eq-bie is a **Fredholm equation of
the second kind**: $\tfrac12 I + K$ is a compact perturbation of a multiple
of the identity, invertible with spectrum clustered around $\tfrac12$. This
has a practical consequence that the learned models inherit: simple
**Richardson iteration**

$$
\mu_{k+1} = \mu_k + \alpha\,\bigl(g - (\tfrac12 I + K)\mu_k\bigr)
$$ {#eq-richardson}

converges geometrically for suitable $\alpha > 0$, with a
resolution-independent iteration count — the operator's spectrum, not the
mesh, sets the rate.

The solution operator then **factorizes**:

$$
\mathcal N_\Gamma
\;=\;
\underbrace{\mathcal D}_{\text{propagation}}
\;\circ\;
\underbrace{\bigl(\tfrac12 I + K\bigr)^{-1}}_{\text{density solve}} .
$$ {#eq-factorization}

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-cap: >
%%|   The BIE factorization. The density solve is a global
%%|   boundary-to-boundary map (second-kind Fredholm, cheap to iterate);
%%|   propagation is a source-to-query integral with an analytic,
%%|   PDE-conforming kernel. The falsification ladder of the learned-BIE
%%|   chapter tests which box carries the operator generalization.
flowchart LR
    g["boundary data g<br/>(on quadrature panels)"] --> S["density solve<br/>(½I + K)μ = g<br/>p Richardson steps"]
    S --> mu["boundary density μ"]
    mu --> P["propagation<br/>u(x) = Σ w_j κ(x−y_j, n_j) μ_j"]
    K["kernel κ<br/>harmonic in x,<br/>exact panel quadrature"] --> S
    K --> P
    P --> u["interior field u(x)<br/>at arbitrary queries"]
```

Both boxes use the *same* kernel $\kappa$: the trace operator $K$ is the
boundary restriction of the propagation kernel. Tying them is not an
aesthetic choice — it is what makes the trace residual of the solve
meaningful as a boundary condition (and, as @sec-ladder shows, tying alone
provides no benefit without the right kernel).

The kernel is singular: in 2D the double-layer kernel is

$$
\partial_{n_y}G(x,y)
= -\frac{1}{2\pi}\,\frac{n_y\cdot(x-y)}{|x-y|^2},
$$

with the panel-integrated singular part equal to a **signed subtended
angle**. Singular kernels demand singular (panel-integrated) quadrature —
midpoint rules near the boundary are wrong by $O(1)$, a fact that refutes
one entire rung of the ladder (H1d in @sec-ladder).

## Harmonicity by construction and the maximum principle

If the propagation kernel is harmonic in $x$ away from the source, then

$$
\Delta_x \sum_j w_j\,\kappa(x - y_j, n_j)\,\mu_j = 0
\quad\text{for \emph{any} density } \mu,
$$

so the predicted field is exactly harmonic no matter what the learned solve
produces. The maximum principle then bounds interior error by boundary trace
error: PDE fidelity holds structurally and only boundary fidelity is left to
learn. In 2D the admissible reflection-invariant exactly-harmonic pair
kernels admit a complete characterization: with

$$
\zeta = n\cdot r + i\,(n\times r), \qquad r = x - y,
$$

$\zeta$ is antiholomorphic in $x$, so $\kappa = \operatorname{Re} F(\zeta)$
is harmonic for any holomorphic $F$; *real* Laurent coefficients make
$\kappa$ even in the pseudoscalar $n \times r$ and hence reflection-safe:

$$
\kappa(r, n)
= \sum_{k\ge1} c_k \operatorname{Re}\zeta^{-k}
+ \sum_{k\ge0} d_k \operatorname{Re}\zeta^{k}.
$$ {#eq-laurent}

The true double-layer kernel is the single member $c_1$ (with the benchmark's
orientation convention, $c_1 = -1/2\pi$), expanded about *each source point*
— there is no global expansion center to break translation covariance. The
hypersingular members $\zeta^{-k}$, $k \ge 2$ are excluded because their
flat-panel principal value does not exist. The 3D analogue is solid harmonics
times Legendre polynomials in $n\cdot\hat r$.

## Well-posedness: which boundary conditions are admissible

The benchmark suites only pose **well-posed** problems:

- **Dirichlet everywhere**: unique solution.
- **Mixed Dirichlet/Neumann**: unique, provided at least one patch is
  Dirichlet (or Robin).
- **Robin** $u + \beta L\,\partial_n u = h$ with dimensionless $\beta > 0$:
  unique.
- **All-Neumann is excluded.** The pure interior Neumann problem determines
  $u$ only up to an additive constant and requires the compatibility
  condition $\int_\Gamma \partial_n u \, dS = 0$; a benchmark that posed it
  without fixing the gauge would score models on an ill-posed target. When
  the program *does* train on Neumann data (@sec-neumann), the targets are
  gauge-fixed to the boundary-measure mean of the exact potential, the model
  reports its output relative to its own exact boundary-trace mean, and the
  discrete flux data satisfy $\sum_j w_j f_j = 0$ exactly.

The Neumann BIE also flips orientation: the interior second-kind operator is
$-\tfrac12 I + K'$ rather than $+\tfrac12 I + K$. For a *learned* solver this
is not a bookkeeping detail: with the wrong gauge, Richardson iteration at
small kernel *diverges*, and SGD will happily exploit that divergence as an
amplifier instead of learning the kernel (@sec-neumann). The general rule —
one of the program's durable findings — is that the jump/orientation
convention must place the zero-kernel initialization inside the solver's
convergent regime.

## Nondimensionalization and the similarity group

Physical problems carry units; learned weights must not. Consider the
similarity action

$$
x' = sRx + t, \qquad s > 0,\quad R \in O(D),
$$

together with $L' = sL$ for the declared reference length and consistent
transformation of all polar-vector fields. Centering at the boundary-measure
centroid $c = \sum_j w_j x_j / \sum_j w_j$ and normalizing

$$
z_j = \frac{x_j - c}{L}, \qquad \omega_j = \frac{w_j}{L^{D-1}}
$$

makes the normalized inputs *invariant* under translation and scale and
*equivariant* under $R$. Every model in the program computes in this frame,
so similarity covariance is exact rather than learned. Two disciplined
consequences:

- the reference length is **only** a geometric nondimensionalizer — the
  constructor rejects a reference length that is also declared as a learned
  field, because exposing the dimensional scale to a learned path would
  defeat the contract;
- what is banned is any length that fails to transform covariantly: a
  fitted constant radius or a training-set length statistic would break scale
  covariance on out-of-distribution sizes without an explicit error. A per-instance
  functional of the input geometry that is itself degree-1 homogeneous —
  the measure-weighted RMS boundary radius the architecture derives
  (@sec-forward-pass) — is valid because it transforms with the data.

The group action also dictates what a propagation kernel may depend on.
Rotating a problem rotates the displacement $x - y$, the boundary normal
$n_y$, and any vector-valued boundary data (a prescribed velocity, a
traction) together; in a homogeneous problem nothing else carries
orientation. The boundary-to-interior map is therefore equivariant under
O($D$), and its rotational symmetry is broken *only* by directional
quantities living on the boundary. A kernel that respects this must be a
function of the **joint invariants** of
$\{x - y,\ n_y,\ \text{boundary vector data}\}$ — magnitudes and pairwise
angles — with vector outputs reconstructed on the local basis those
directions span, never read off an absolute frame. GLOBE (arXiv
[2511.15856](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.15856)) articulated exactly this
structure for boundary-driven PDE surrogates: positions enter only as
relative displacements, all input vectors are reduced to joint rotation
invariants, and equivariant vector outputs are recovered by reprojection
onto bases built from the input directions. The double-layer kernel above,
$-\tfrac{1}{2\pi}\,n_y\cdot(x-y)/|x-y|^2$, already has this form — a joint
invariant of $n_y$ and $x - y$, with no reference to an absolute frame.

For parametric PDEs the same discipline applies to coefficients: the screened
operator $\Delta u - \kappa^2 u = 0$ enters through the dimensionless group
$\tilde\kappa = \kappa L$, and — as @sec-parametric establishes — belongs
*analytically inside the kernel basis* ($K_0(\tilde\kappa\rho)$,
$K_1(\tilde\kappa\rho)$), not inside a learned conditioning network. (When
the operator is unknown that rule inverts into a limitation statement; see
the closing note of @sec-parametric.)

## What remains when the PDE is unknown {#sec-pde-agnostic}

Under the product scope the governing equations are not given, and for the
eventual targets they are not perfectly knowable. It is worth stating
precisely which parts of the BIE story are properties of the *problem class*
— well-posed, homogeneous, same equations everywhere — and which are
properties of the *known fundamental solution*, because only the former can
be assumed in the product setting.

**PDE-agnostic, assumable in deployment:**

- the **factorization** @eq-factorization of the solution operator into a
  boundary-to-boundary density solve composed with a source-to-query
  propagation — nothing in it names Laplace;
- the **second-kind solve structure** @eq-richardson, together with its
  jump/orientation gauge rule (the zero-kernel initialization must sit
  inside the solver's convergent regime);
- the **exact contracts**: linearity in the drive where the physics is
  linear, similarity covariance, quadrature weighting against boundary
  measure, all-to-all information flow, query independence;
- **similarity-equivariant kernels of relative geometry**,
  $\kappa(x - y,\, n_y)$. Homogeneity plus identical equations everywhere
  means the propagation rule cannot depend on absolute position *or absolute
  orientation*: it is translation-invariant through the displacement
  $x - y$ and equivariant under rotations and reflections, with rotational
  symmetry broken only by directional data on the boundary — so $\kappa$
  is a function of the joint invariants of
  $\{x - y,\ n_y,\ \text{boundary vector data}\}$. The entire domain
  dependence is carried by the density solve. This is the one strong
  structural assumption the problem class licenses;
- the **singular-quadrature discipline**: whatever the kernel family turns
  out to be, its near-boundary singular structure must be integrated
  exactly, not sampled (the H1d refutation of @sec-ladder).

**PDE-specific, available on the benchmarks but not in deployment:**

- the particular fundamental-solution family — the harmonic Laurent basis
  @eq-laurent, the Yukawa Bessel kernels of @sec-parametric, solid harmonics
  in 3D — and with it the derived guarantees: exact harmonicity of the
  predicted field and the maximum-principle bound on interior error. These
  exist because the benchmark PDEs were chosen with known answers.

In the product setting the kernel family must therefore be *learned* — at
most biased toward typical-PDE behavior through a singularity dictionary
(@sec-future) — and PDE fidelity becomes a property to be earned from data
rather than imposed by construction.
